analysis.one_liner: Cuts the capital gains tax rate to 15 percent and adjusts investment gains for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a vote before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut the tax rate on long-term capital gains from 28 percent to 15 percent for individuals and from 34 percent to 15 percent for corporations [S2][S3]. It also would have cut the alternative minimum tax rate on gains, including a 7.5 percent rate for gains earned by lower- and middle-income taxpayers [S2][S3]. Finally, it would have adjusted the purchase price of stocks and business property for inflation, so taxes would apply only to real gains, not gains caused by rising prices [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who realize capital gains — mainly holders of corporate stock and business property, who are concentrated among higher-income households — would pay a sharply lower tax rate (15 percent instead of 28 percent for individuals, 15 percent instead of 34 percent for corporations) and would pay tax only on gains above inflation [S2][S3]. Lower- and middle-income taxpayers with gains would pay 7.5 percent on an initial portion of their gains [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the top individual capital gains rate from 28 percent to 15 percent, and applies a 7.5 percent rate to the portion of net capital gain that falls within the lower brackets for lower- and middle-income taxpayers [S2][S3].
Cuts the corporate capital gains rate from 34 percent to 15 percent [S2][S3].
Reduces the alternative minimum tax rate on capital gains to match, so the minimum tax could not claw back the cut [S2][S3].
Indexes the basis of corporate stock and business property held more than one year to the gross national product deflator, so tax is owed only on gains exceeding inflation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenues would fall by the amount of the rate cut and indexing; that lost revenue must be made up by other taxpayers, by borrowing, or by reduced government spending. The benefit flows overwhelmingly to the shrinking group of households that realize large capital gains each year.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no revenue offset: cutting rates to 15 percent and indexing gains would reduce federal revenue, and that cost would be borne by other taxpayers or by government programs [S3].

The bill's benefits concentrate on holders of corporate stock and business property, since it indexes only those assets — not homes or most other personal property — and cuts rates on gains that flow mainly to investors with substantial assets [S3].
A good-faith supporter would acknowledge that the bill offers no offsetting tax increase or spending cut, so its fiscal cost would have added to deficits at a time of budget pressure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a large, immediate tax reduction to investors in stocks and business assets, with a smaller benefit to lower- and middle-income taxpayers who realize gains. The cost is an unoffset loss of federal revenue that other taxpayers would eventually bear, and the design concentrates the benefit on those with the most appreciated assets. It is a genuine tax cut, but its incidence is steeply tilted toward wealthier households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and no chamber ever voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Kolbe introduced the bill on February 3, 1993, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law [S1][S5].
Thirty-five representatives signed on as cosponsors — 32 Republicans and 3 Democrats [S4].
The action record shows no further activity: no committee vote, no floor action, and no Senate companion action through the end of the 103rd Congress in January 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, capital gains tax rates stayed at 28 percent for individuals and 34 percent for corporations, and the Treasury kept that revenue. Investors with large gains are worse off than they would have been under the bill; the lower- and middle-income 7.5 percent rate also never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; capital gains rates stayed at 28%

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on it; no markup, no committee vote, no report to the floor [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Republican — 32 of 35 cosponsors were Republicans, with 3 Democrats — and no House vote was ever taken.

industries.note: A 15 percent rate on individual capital gains plus inflation indexing would sharply cut taxes on stock profits, and the bill extends the indexing benefit through mutual funds and other pooled vehicles. Because the cut is not offset, its cost shifts to other taxpayers and the federal budget.

The bill cuts the corporate capital gains rate from 34 percent to 15 percent and lowers related corporate tax rates on certain securities transactions, directly reducing corporate tax bills on asset sales.

industries.industry: Real estate investment trusts and business property owners
industries.note: Business tangible property and REIT interests would get inflation-indexed basis, letting owners pay tax only on real gains. This mainly benefits holders of commercial and investment real estate rather than homeowners, whose homes are not indexed under the bill.
